## `stabilis.bench.graph`

Can this bench separate its oscillators at all? And if not, what fixes it?

Under independence a measurement of sources `i` and `j` through channel `c`
has, at each tau,

    sigma2_meas = sigma2_i + sigma2_j + sigma2_c

so the source block of the design matrix is the **unsigned** incidence
matrix of the graph whose vertices are sources and whose edges are
measurements. Its rank is a graph property:

    rank = n_sources - (number of bipartite connected components)

which gives the result this whole module exists for:

> **A connected set of measurements determines its sources' individual
> variances if and only if it contains an odd cycle.**

That is not a curiosity. It is *why the technique is called
three-cornered hat*: a triangle is the smallest odd cycle. Four oscillators
measured round a ring A-B, B-C, C-D, D-A form a 4-cycle, which is
bipartite, so **that setup determines nothing about any individual
oscillator however long it runs** -- and one diagonal fixes it. A chain of
measurements is a tree, also bipartite, also hopeless.

Users get this wrong constantly and no tool tells them; they return a
number from an underdetermined system, or silently regularize. This one
refuses, says which combination is unidentifiable, and names the single
extra measurement that would fix it -- **before any data is collected**,
which is when the answer is still cheap to act on.

**A back-to-back run pins its own channel and contributes nothing to
separating sources.** So a bench made only of noise-floor runs is perfectly
well-conditioned in its channel block and completely useless in its source
block. That is a real mistake people make, and `check` says so in as many
words.

Why the parity argument works: an unsigned incidence row is `e_i + e_j`.
Assign each vertex `+1` or `-1` by a 2-colouring; then for every edge of a
bipartite component the two endpoints differ in colour, so the vector `v`
with `v_k` = the colour is orthogonal to every row -- a null direction, and
exactly the "shift all of one side up and the other down" ambiguity. An odd
cycle makes the 2-colouring impossible, and the null direction with it.

#### `design_matrix`

```python
design_matrix(bench: Bench)
```

`(A, sources, free_channels, known)` for `A @ v = b - known`.

One row per measurement: `1` in each of its two source columns, `1` in
its channel column. Two conventions carry real weight:

* **A back-to-back row is `0` across every source.** Writing
  `A[row, a] += 1` twice would be wrong -- both ends are the same
  oscillator, so its noise is common to both and cancels in the
  difference rather than doubling.
* **A channel whose `floor` is declared gets no column.** It is a known
  constant, so it moves to the right-hand side in `known` instead of
  consuming a degree of freedom. This is what makes the classical
  three-cornered hat work: three sources through one channel is four
  unknowns against three rows and hopeless, but declaring
  `Channel(floor=0.0)` -- the assumption the classical method makes
  silently -- leaves three unknowns and three rows, which is exactly
  determined. The assumption becomes something the user writes down
  rather than something the algorithm hides.

Built without touching a single data file, which is what lets `check`
run while the experiment is still being planned.

#### `check`

```python
check(bench: Bench) -> Identifiability
```

Full identifiability verdict. Reads no data files.

Runs before an experiment, not after it -- which is the whole value.

#### `derivable_edges`

```python
derivable_edges(bench: Bench) -> tuple[tuple[str, str, str, str, str], ...]
```

Pairs obtainable by subtracting two records rather than measuring one.

**The odd-cycle theorem is about the variances, not about the records.**
Given `x_ac` and `x_bc` as time series, `x_ab = x_ac - x_bc` identically,
because the common reference cancels. So any two sources measured against
a shared third are one subtraction away from a third edge -- and that
edge closes a triangle, which is an odd cycle, which is exactly what a
bipartite component was missing.

This is not a trick, it is *how the three-cornered hat is normally run*:
two counters against the house clock, and the third pair formed in
software. It also means the common reference need not be special. C can
be the local clock everything is plugged into, and the hat still returns
`sigma_C` -- the reference is an unknown like any other.

Two conditions the graph cannot check, and which the report states
rather than assumes:

* **Simultaneity.** The subtraction is only meaningful if the two
  records overlap in time on a common timebase. `Measurement` carries an
  epoch string and no duration, so claiming to verify that here would be
  inventing a capability -- the same reason `_overlapping_epochs` only
  trusts exact equality.
* **The channel term.** A derived record carries the noise of *both*
  contributing channels: `Var = sigma2_a + sigma2_b + sigma2_c1 +
  sigma2_c2`. A `Measurement` names one channel, so the design row would
  count one. Declare the floors -- zero is the classical hat's silent
  assumption -- or give the derived row its own channel whose floor is
  the sum.

#### `suggest_edge`

```python
suggest_edge(bench: Bench) -> tuple[tuple[str, str], ...]
```

Pairs whose measurement would most improve identifiability.

Every pair not already measured is tried, the rank recomputed, and the
ones giving the largest increase are returned. Directly actionable --
"measure B against D" -- and cheap, because the search is over pairs of
sources rather than anything involving data.

Ties are common and are all returned: on a 4-cycle either diagonal
works, and saying so is more useful than picking one arbitrarily.

## `stabilis.bench.model`

The bench: which oscillator, against which, through which instrument.

Every other tool treats a measurement as an anonymous column of numbers.
But `x_ab(t)` is never just a column -- it is *this* source against *that*
one, through *this* channel of *that* device. Once the program knows that,
four things become mechanical rather than manual: the N-cornered hat,
instrument noise-floor subtraction, common-mode detection, and the honest
refusal that says a setup cannot separate its oscillators no matter how
long it runs.

Data only. No behaviour beyond validation, and **`stats/` must never import
`bench/`** -- an AST test enforces it, the same independence discipline the
certified oracle has. The estimators must stay usable, and testable, with
no notion of where their data came from.

Two conventions that look like mistakes and are not:

* **`source_a == source_b` is legal.** That is a back-to-back run, both
  ends of the measurement on one source, and it is how a channel's noise
  floor gets *measured* rather than assumed. It contributes nothing to
  separating oscillators and everything to pinning its channel.
* **`spec_adev` is a vendor's claim, not a measurement.** It is carried so
  a result can be plotted against the specification the part was bought to
  meet, and it is never mixed into a fit. The validation-integrity rule
  applies to datasheet points exactly as it does to published tables.

#### `SCHEMA_VERSION`

```python
SCHEMA_VERSION = 1
```

Bumped when the JSON layout changes in a way an older reader would misread. `store.load` refuses a version it does not know rather than guessing at the difference.

#### `Device`

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Device
```

A measurement instrument, owning its channels.

Channels belong to a device rather than floating free because that
ownership is what makes the common-mode check possible: two channels of
one device share a timebase, an LO, a power supply and a thermal
environment, so their noise is common and does not cancel.

## `stabilis.bench.recommend`

Which technique this bench supports, read off the graph.

`check` answers "can the hat separate these oscillators". That is the
wrong question to ask on its own, because the hat is not the only thing a
bench can do and it is not always the thing that should be done. There are
two techniques and **they are not alternatives** -- they remove different
unknowns:

|                        | separates the sources | removes the channel term |
|------------------------|-----------------------|--------------------------|
| N-cornered hat         | yes, given an odd cycle | no: declare the floor, or measure it back-to-back |
| cross-correlation      | no                    | yes, in expectation, declaring nothing |

The design matrix has a column per source and a column per undeclared
channel. The odd cycle is what makes the source columns solvable; a
repeated edge is what makes a channel column *unnecessary*. A bench that
has both needs neither assumption.

That composition is the useful part, and it is concrete: measure A against
B **twice, through two independent channels**, and the cross-variance of
those two records estimates `sigma2_A + sigma2_B` with the channel noise
rejected. That is a hat row with no channel term. For the classical
three-cornered hat -- three sources through one channel, four unknowns
against three rows, hopeless -- one such repeated edge closes the system
without anyone having to assert that the channel is silent.
`would_identify` computes exactly that, by adding the derived row to a
hypothetical bench and re-running `check`.

**The correction this module exists to make.** It is tempting, and it was
written down here in an earlier draft, that two channels of one instrument
are the *good* case for cross-correlation because the shared instrument
noise is what you want to reject. That is backwards. Cross-correlation
rejects the part of the channel noise that is **independent** between the
two channels; the part they share -- one timebase, one LO, one supply, one
oven -- passes straight through:

    x_1 = x_ab + n_common + n_1'
    x_2 = x_ab + n_common + n_2'
    E[d_1 d_2] = Var(x_ab) + Var(n_common)

So two channels of one device is *better than one channel* and *worse than
two devices*, and the residual is not something more data fixes -- it is a
floor. **Independent instruments are better for both techniques.** What is
true of the same-device case is only that it is a configuration
cross-correlation can use at all and the hat cannot, since both records
name the same source pair.

#### `CrossOpportunity`

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CrossOpportunity
```

One source pair measured through more than one channel.

*Fields*

```python
source_a: str
source_b: str
measurements: tuple[str, ...]
channels: tuple[str, ...]
devices: tuple[str, ...]
quality: str
```

*property* `clean(self) -> bool`

#### `Recommendation`

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Recommendation
```

What this bench can do, and which assumption each answer rests on.

*Fields*

```python
opportunities: tuple[CrossOpportunity, ...]
hat_identifiable: bool
hat_deficiency: int
would_identify: bool
channels_determined: tuple[str, ...]
notes: tuple[str, ...]
```

*property* `has_cross(self) -> bool`

*method* `report(self) -> str`

#### `cross_opportunities`

```python
cross_opportunities(bench: Bench) -> tuple[CrossOpportunity, ...]
```

Source pairs measured through two or more distinct channels.

Back-to-back rows are included: two channels measuring the *same*
source against itself cross-correlate to the source's own variance
with both channels rejected, which is the purest form of the technique
and the one a phase-noise test set implements in hardware.

Two records through *one* channel are not an opportunity. One channel
cannot make two simultaneous measurements, so either they are the same
record described twice or they ran at different times -- and neither
gives two independent views of one interval.

#### `recommend`

```python
recommend(bench: Bench) -> Recommendation
```

Which technique this bench supports, and whether they compose.

Reads no data files, for the same reason `check` does not: the answer
is worth most while the experiment is still being planned. "Run that
pair again on the other counter" is cheap advice on a Tuesday.

## `stabilis.bench.solve`

One linear solve per tau, subsuming three features that are usually three.

    sigma2_meas = sigma2_i + sigma2_j + sigma2_channel

is linear in the variances and non-negative by physics, so the whole bench
is `A @ v = b`, `v >= 0` -- exactly non-negative least squares, solved
exactly by `_nnls`. Three named techniques are special cases of the same
solve rather than separate code:

* **three-cornered hat** is the 3-source triangle;
* **N-cornered hat** is any larger graph containing an odd cycle;
* **instrument noise-floor subtraction** is what a back-to-back row does --
  both ends on one source, so it drops out of every source column and pins
  only its channel.

**Any estimator that is a variance works for free**, because the sum rule
holds for anything that is one. What the solver refuses is anything whose
result says `is_variance=False` -- MTIE, because the maximum of a sum is
not the sum of maxima, and TIE rms, because it retains a frequency offset
that is deterministic rather than adding in quadrature. Two different
failures, checked by one flag.

**Negative variances are reported, not clipped.** The unconstrained
least-squares solution is computed alongside the constrained one and
returned signed. A negative source variance is the system saying an
assumption is violated -- the sources are not independent, or one is
misattributed, or a channel is worse than believed. Clipping it to zero
destroys the single most useful diagnostic the method produces, which is
why the NNLS answer and the signed one are both on the result.

#### `REFUSED_KINDS`

```python
REFUSED_KINDS = frozenset({'mtie', 'tierms'})
```

Statistics that are not variances, detected by the result's own `is_variance` flag rather than by name so a plugin estimator cannot slip past. The names below are for the error message only.  The two this library ships fail for *different* reasons, and saying "extreme-value statistics" of both would be wrong. MTIE is one: the maximum of a sum is not the sum of maxima. TIE rms is a mean square and its stochastic part does obey the sum rule -- it is refused because it retains the frequency offset between the sources, which is deterministic, so two clocks 1e-12 off can differ by 2e-12 or by nothing depending on sign. Neither combines the way this solver assumes.

#### `BenchSolution`

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BenchSolution
```

Per-tau variances for every source and every free channel.

*Fields*

```python
tau_s: np.ndarray
sources: tuple[str, ...]
channels: tuple[str, ...]
source_var: np.ndarray
channel_var: np.ndarray
unconstrained: np.ndarray
residual: np.ndarray
kkt: np.ndarray
estimator: str

```

*method* `dev(self, source_id: str) -> np.ndarray`

Deviation for one source. Zero where the fit pinned it at zero.

*method* `signed_var(self, source_id: str) -> np.ndarray`

The *unconstrained* variance for one source, sign intact.

*property* `any_negative(self) -> bool`

#### `common_mode_warnings`

```python
common_mode_warnings(bench: Bench) -> tuple[str, ...]
```

Correlations the bench can see, each naming its own evidence.

The whole system rests on the off-diagonal terms vanishing, and these
are the common ways they do not. Warnings rather than refusals: they
are statements about the physics that the graph cannot settle on its
own, and the user may know better.

#### `solve`

```python
solve(bench: Bench, results: dict, require_identifiable: bool=True) -> BenchSolution
```

Solve the bench at every tau the measurements have in common.

`results` maps `Measurement.id` to a `StabilityResult` -- computed by
the caller, with whatever estimator and settings it likes, which is how
"any variance works" stays true without this module knowing anything
about estimators.

`require_identifiable=False` solves anyway and lets NNLS return the
minimum-norm-ish answer among the many that fit. It exists because a
user may want to see the fit for a bench they know is degenerate, and
it warns loudly. The default refuses, with the diagnostic that names
the measurement which would fix it.

## `stabilis.bench.store`

`bench.json`: one file, schema-versioned, referencing data rather than holding it.

Plain JSON and human-editable on purpose. A bench is a description of an
experiment, and the person who ran the experiment has to be able to read it,
correct it, and diff it in a pull request without this library in the loop.

**Data is referenced by path and SHA-256, never contained.** `load` can then
verify that every file still hashes to what the bench says, and refuse to
analyse a bench whose data has moved underneath it -- a measurement whose
bytes changed is a different measurement, and silently analysing it would
put an unearned signature on the result. Verification is opt-in at load and
strict when asked, because a bench is often written before the data exists.

No pickle, ever, for the reason in `CLAUDE.md`: a bench file arriving from a
customer's rig is untrusted input, and JSON cannot execute.

#### `HashMismatch`

```python
class HashMismatch
```

A referenced data file no longer hashes to what the bench recorded.

#### `to_dict`

```python
to_dict(bench: Bench) -> dict
```

JSON-ready, with tuples as lists and no numpy anywhere.

Writes `created` exactly as the bench carries it, including empty. A
serializer that invents a timestamp is inventing data, and this one is
also used for hashing and diffing, where a value that changes on every
call is actively harmful. `save` does the stamping, visibly.

#### `from_dict`

```python
from_dict(data: dict, path: str='') -> Bench
```

Rebuild a bench, refusing a schema this reader does not know.

Refusing an unknown version rather than best-guessing it is the whole
point of having the field: a reader that guesses will one day guess
wrong on a customer's file and produce a plausible answer.

#### `save`

```python
save(bench: Bench, path, stamp_created: bool=True) -> Bench
```

Write `bench.json` and return the bench as written.

Returns the bench rather than the path because saving can change it:
an unstamped bench gets a `created` time here, and the caller needs the
object that matches the file rather than the one it passed in.

`stamp_created=False` for a byte-reproducible write -- regenerating a
fixture, or hashing a bench for provenance, where a timestamp that
changes on every call would make the output differ from itself.

#### `load`

```python
load(path, verify_hashes: bool=False) -> Bench
```

Read a bench. `verify_hashes=True` refuses if any file has changed.

Off by default because benches are routinely written *before* the data
exists -- that is the point of `bench check`. On when a solve is about
to happen, where analysing the wrong bytes is the failure that matters.

#### `verify`

```python
verify(bench: Bench) -> list[str]
```

Every mismatch between a recorded hash and the file on disk.

Returns a list rather than raising so a caller can report all of them
at once; chasing these one exception at a time is miserable.

A measurement with no `sha256` is skipped and *said to be* skipped by
the caller -- absence is not agreement, and treating an unhashed row as
verified would quietly defeat the whole mechanism.
